# Reference snapshot fixture

A small, deterministic, hand-checkable snapshot committed for two purposes:

1. **Downstream consumers.** A reader of Wake snapshots can be developed and
   tested against this fixture without a live daemon, root, or a kernel. It is
   the only executable artefact Wake ships a consumer (SPEC.md §6.2) — see
   `../../../docs/snapshot-format.md` for the contract it demonstrates, and §6
   there for what a conforming consumer must do.
2. **Schema drift detection.** `internal/snapshot/fixture_test.go` validates this
   fixture against the live `snapshot` package types (`Manifest`, `SystemInfo`,
   `event.Event`) on every `go test ./internal/snapshot/...`. If a future change to
   those types is incompatible with this fixture's shape, that test fails —
   catching an accidental schema break before it ships.

## Scenario

A fictional `smtpd` process (`pid 4321`, unit `mstr.service`) execs, fails to open
a certificate it does not have permission to read, and is then killed by
`SIGKILL`. A `watched-process` trigger rule named `mstr-crash` fires on the exit,
producing this snapshot. A containerised `curl` and an OOM kill appear alongside
it so that the enrichment triple and the memory fields are exercised too.

## Coverage

The fixture contains **one event of every class**, deliberately:

| Class | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `exec` | argv present; a second one with `argv_truncated` set |
| `exit` | death by signal, with `exit_signal` and `signal_name` |
| `signal` | delivery with a `sender_pid` |
| `oom` | the memory figures the tracepoint reports |
| `open` | a **failing** syscall, with `ret` and `errno` together |
| `connect` | a failed attempt, with the state transition and container attribution |
| `generic` | a record the decoder did not recognise, raw payload retained |

`generic` matters most. It is the class a happy-path fixture would omit, and the
one a naive consumer is most likely to discard — which re-creates the silent
loss the class exists to prevent, at exactly the moment the kernel is producing
something unexpected.

The manifest also reports a **non-zero drop count** (`userspace_ring.open`). An
all-zero report would let a consumer satisfy the "surface non-zero drops"
obligation (`docs/snapshot-format.md` §6.3) by accident, having never seen a
snapshot that admits to losing anything.

## Contents

```
reference-snapshot/
├── manifest.json       # see docs/snapshot-format.md §2
├── events.jsonl.zst     # 8 events, oldest first — see docs/snapshot-format.md §3
├── system.json          # see docs/snapshot-format.md §4
└── proc/                # see docs/snapshot-format.md §5
    ├── status
    ├── limits
    ├── cgroup
    ├── cmdline
    └── fd_listing.txt
```

Decompress `events.jsonl.zst` with any standard zstd tool, e.g.:

```
unzstd -c reference-snapshot/events.jsonl.zst
```

## Provenance and regeneration

Generated by the real `snapshot.Writer` — the same code path a live daemon uses
— against fixed fake inputs (a fixed clock, `SystemInfoSource` and
`ProcSource`), so its bytes are what the package actually produces rather than
what someone believed it produced.

```
make fixture
```

The generator is `internal/snapshot/mkfixture`. Everything that would otherwise
vary is pinned, so regenerating an unchanged tree is byte-for-byte a no-op.

`config_hash` is a placeholder (`fixture000...`), not a real hash, since this
fixture has no accompanying `wake.toml`.

**Regenerating is not the remedy for a failing schema test.** If a test reports
that this fixture no longer matches the code, then the code changed the
serialised form of a public contract. See `CHANGELOG.md`, "Before you bump it".
